candidates.stimulus_use: The GP viewpoint and 'what is left over' suggested looking at what an injury-focused emergency department visit leaves unanswered, and the 48-hour timescale suggested the GP's window to act on the letter.
candidates.working_title: 'No bony injury' is half a letter
candidates.core_insight: An emergency department letter after a fall without injury is a prompt for the GP to arrange a falls assessment, because the attendance itself marks a person at higher risk of falling again.
candidates.angle: The emergency department answers one question (is anything broken?) and the GP inherits another (why did they fall, and will they fall again?). The letter that answers the first often reads like a closed case. From the GP's side, the days after the letter arrives are the chance to act.
candidates.position: A GP who receives an emergency department discharge letter for a fall should treat it as a trigger for a multifactorial falls assessment, whether or not there was an injury.
claims_needing_evidence: Older people who attend an emergency department after a fall have a high rate of further falls in the following year (cohort data or control arms of ED falls trials, e.g. PROFET).

UK guidance recommends a multifactorial falls risk assessment for older people who present for medical attention because of a fall or who have fallen in the past 12 months (NICE NG249 text; check exact criteria).

The World Falls Guidelines 2022 place people who present with a fall-related injury, or with specified severity markers, in the high-risk group that should receive multifactorial assessment (Montero-Odasso 2022, Age and Ageing).

A randomised trial of multifactorial assessment and intervention for older people attending an ED after a fall reduced subsequent falls, and later ED-based trials had mixed results (Close 1999 Lancet; systematic review of ED-based interventions).

candidates.follow: The account turns routine paperwork into clinical decisions.

candidates.stimulus_use: The 'counting' process and the change-of-scale operation suggested the difference between counting falls (events) and counting fallers (people).
candidates.working_title: Fewer falls, or fewer people falling?
candidates.core_insight: Falls trials report two different counts, the number of falls and the number of people who fell, and an intervention can reduce the first by more than the second.
candidates.angle: Counting events and counting people are two scales for the same trial. In the Cochrane review of exercise, the reduction in the rate of falls is larger than the reduction in the number of people who fall, because some people fall many times. Quoting only the larger figure overstates what one person can expect.
candidates.position: Anyone quoting a falls prevention result should say whether it is a rate of falls or a proportion of people who fell, and give the absolute numbers.
claims_needing_evidence: In the 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for community-dwelling older people, exercise reduced the rate of falls by about [N to verify]% (rate ratio) and the number of people having one or more falls by about [N to verify]% (risk ratio) (Sherrington 2019 Cochrane).
The review's absolute estimates were about [N to verify] fewer falls per 1000 person-years and [N to verify] fewer fallers per 1000 people (Cochrane summary of findings table).
Falls are unevenly distributed, with a minority of people having repeated falls (prospective cohort data; falls trial methodology papers).
The ProFaNE consensus recommends that falls trials report the rate of falls, the proportion of fallers and fall-related injuries as separate outcomes (Lamb 2005, J Am Geriatr Soc).

candidates.opening_line_draft: A falls trial can report fewer falls without reporting fewer people who fell, and the two results mean different things.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison of two icon arrays built only from the Cochrane summary of findings: left, falls per 1000 person-years with and without exercise; right, people with one or more falls per 1000 people; both labelled with denominators, time period and source.
candidates.pause: Practitioners who quote 'exercise cuts falls by about a quarter' see that there is a second, smaller figure.
candidates.gain: A habit for reading and quoting any falls study accurately.
candidates.follow: The account explains how to read the evidence, as well as what it says.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E065 quoted the Cochrane fall-rate reduction of about a quarter. This post is about the difference between the two outcomes in that review and how to read them; it makes no new claim for exercise.

candidates.stimulus_use: The 'first hour' timescale and the change of scale from population figures to one person's time on the floor suggested asking whether an individual can get up, and practising it in advance.
candidates.working_title: Can you get up off the floor?
candidates.core_insight: Being unable to get up after a fall is common and harmful, and getting up from the floor is a skill that a physiotherapist can assess and help a person practise before it is needed.
candidates.angle: The population figure (a large share of older people who fall can't get up unaided) becomes one person's first hour on the floor. The useful action is to find out now, while well, and to practise.
candidates.position: Anyone who has fallen, or who feels unsteady, should ask to be shown how to get up from the floor and to practise it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a community cohort, about [N to verify] of older people who fell without serious injury were unable to get up without help (Tinetti 1993, JAMA).
Inability to get up after a fall was associated with later decline in daily activities, hospital admission and moves into long-term care (Tinetti 1993; Fleming 2008, BMJ).
The World Falls Guidelines 2022 treat lying on the floor and being unable to get up as a marker of high falls risk that calls for a full assessment (Montero-Odasso 2022).

Physiotherapists teach a staged method of getting up from the floor, sometimes by backward chaining, and small studies report that older people can learn it (Reece and Simpson 1996; Adams and Tyson 2000) (unsure).
Some UK falls prevention programmes, such as FaME, include practice of getting down to and up from the floor (programme description; Skelton 2005).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Has anyone ever asked whether you can get up off the floor on your own?

candidates.pause: A plain question that most readers have never been asked.
candidates.gain: A specific thing to request and practise.
candidates.follow: Practical advice that changes what happens on a bad day.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. E078 and E166 were about alarms; no earlier post covered getting up from the floor.

candidates.stimulus_use: The service-aim operation applied to hospital discharge, with the occupational therapist viewpoint and the 'first month' timescale, pointed to the weeks after discharge; the thermostat and choir-singing words gave nothing usable.
candidates.core_insight: The weeks after discharge from hospital are a period of high falls risk, and a few steps in that month (a home hazard check, restarting strength and balance work, reviewing medicines changed in hospital) have evidence behind them.
candidates.angle: The stated aim of discharge is a safe return home. What people experience is a weakened body in an unchanged house, often with new medicines. From an occupational therapist's view, the home is where the discharge plan is tested.
candidates.position: Every older person discharged after a fall or a long admission should have a named plan for the first month at home that covers the house, exercise and medicines.
claims_needing_evidence: The rate of falls is raised in the weeks after hospital discharge compared with other times (Mahoney 2000, Arch Intern Med; post-discharge cohort studies) (N and time period to verify).
In older people with a history of falls, home visits by an occupational therapist to assess and modify hazards reduced falls in a randomised trial (Cumming 1999, J Am Geriatr Soc).

A systematic review of falls prevention after hospital discharge found home hazard modification reduced falls in higher-risk people, with less clear evidence for other interventions in that period (Naseri 2018, Age and Ageing) (verify).
Medicines started in hospital, including sedatives, sometimes continue after discharge without review (medicines reconciliation studies) (unsure of best source).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Coming home from hospital is one of the likeliest times for an older person to fall. The first month at home needs a plan of its own.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram of the first four weeks at home with three verified elements: a home hazard check by an occupational therapist, restarting strength and balance exercise, and a review of medicines changed in hospital; source credits in the footer.
candidates.pause: Families and discharge teams recognise the first weeks home as the anxious period.
candidates.gain: A short list of what to ask for before and after discharge.
candidates.follow: The account shows what good care looks like in the gaps between services.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E068 covered home hazard work by occupational therapists and E145 hospital sleeping tablets continuing at home. This post is about the post-discharge window as a distinct high-risk period and the plan for it.

candidates.stimulus_use: Reversing the default assumption that a lower falls count means safer care, seen from a service manager's averaged monthly rates, gave the argument about what the metric rewards.
candidates.working_title: A falls rate that improves for the wrong reason
candidates.core_insight: A ward or care home falls rate can go down because people are kept in bed or in a chair, so falls figures need to be read alongside a measure of how much people are moving.
candidates.angle: Most falls happen when people move, so the easiest way to lower a falls rate is less movement. A service manager who sees only falls per 1000 bed days can't tell good falls prevention from enforced immobility, which carries its own harms.
candidates.position: Services that report falls rates should also report a measure of mobility, such as how many patients walk or get up and dressed each day. (Judgement, marked as such.)
claims_needing_evidence: Older people in hospital spend most of their time lying in bed, including many who can walk: about [N to verify]% of the time in one study (Brown 2009, J Am Geriatr Soc).
Low mobility in hospital is associated with loss of function and new disability after discharge (Brown 2004, J Am Geriatr Soc; Covinsky 2011, JAMA).

Clinicians have described a tension between falls prevention measures and mobility in hospital, including bed rest orders, alarms and instructions not to get up (Growdon, Shorr and Inouye 2017, JAMA Intern Med).
Hospital falls are commonly reported as falls per 1000 occupied bed days (national audit methodology, e.g. RCP National Audit of Inpatient Falls) (verify).

candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: two drawn ward dashboards side by side, labelled 'Illustrative, no real data'. One shows only 'falls per 1000 bed days'; the other shows falls beside 'patients who walked today' and 'patients up and dressed'.
candidates.pause: Managers and nurses who report the figure recognise the incentive.
candidates.gain: A specific second measure to put beside the falls rate.
candidates.follow: The account examines what services measure and what that measurement rewards.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E081 covered the causes of hospital falls and E166 bed and chair alarms. This post is about how the falls metric can reward immobility and does not repeat the alarm argument.

candidates.stimulus_use: The aviation-checklist domain and the 'first minute' timescale suggested a short structured check before helping someone up; the operation asked which findings would change that decision.
candidates.working_title: The first minute after finding someone on the floor
candidates.core_insight: Before helping someone up after a fall, a few checks decide whether to call an ambulance or coach them to get up themselves, and lifting a person bodily risks injuring both people.
candidates.angle: A pre-action checklist for families and care workers: ask what would change the decision to help them up (new head, neck or back pain, can't move a limb, unconscious at any point, chest pain or breathing difficulty, a head knock while on a blood thinner). If none apply, help them get up using a sturdy chair, and don't lift them.
candidates.position: Families and care workers should use a short structured check before helping someone up after a fall, and should not lift a fallen person bodily.
claims_needing_evidence: NHS and first-aid guidance advises not moving someone who may have a neck or back injury or who can't move a limb, and calling 999 (NHS inform or NHS website; St John Ambulance).

Care homes in parts of England use a structured tool (ISTUMBLE) to decide whether a fallen resident can be helped up or needs an ambulance (ambulance service or NHS guidance) (unsure of the exact items).
Moving and handling guidance advises against manually lifting a person from the floor because of the risk of injury to carers (Health and Safety Executive guidance).
An uninjured person can often get up with coaching using a sturdy chair, following the method in physiotherapy guides (Chartered Society of Physiotherapy; NHS inform).
evidence_leads: NHS inform (Scotland) or NHS website page on what to do after a fall (unsure of page title)

candidates.opening_line_draft: If you find someone on the floor after a fall, spend the first minute checking them before anyone tries to help them up.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card with five yes or no checks taken word for word from one verified source (for example: new head, neck or back pain; can't move an arm or leg; was unconscious; chest pain or trouble breathing; hit their head and takes a blood thinner). 'Any yes: call 999 and keep them warm.' 'All no: help them get up by themselves using a chair.'
candidates.pause: Carers and care workers face this exact moment and rarely have a clear rule for it.
candidates.gain: A decision they can make calmly in the first minute.
candidates.follow: Practical, checkable advice for carers and care staff.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Earlier falls posts covered assessment after the event; none covered the decision made on the floor.

candidates.stimulus_use: Asking which single fact would change the decision after a fall with a knock to the head led to anticoagulant use.
candidates.working_title: The blood thinner and the knock to the head
candidates.core_insight: An older person who takes an anticoagulant and hits their head in a fall should get medical advice the same day, because UK head injury guidance recommends a scan for people on anticoagulants even when they seem well.
candidates.angle: The one fact that most changes what happens after a head knock is whether the person takes a blood thinner. Families should say it first, by name, to whoever they call.
candidates.position: If someone who takes an anticoagulant knocks their head in a fall, the family should seek same-day medical advice and name the medicine.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE head injury guidance recommends CT head scanning within [time to verify] for people with a head injury who take anticoagulants, even without other indications (NICE NG232, 2023; check whether the wording is 'perform' or 'consider' and which medicines are included).
Bleeding inside the skull after head injury is more likely in people taking anticoagulants than in similar people not taking them (cohort studies or systematic review).
Scottish head injury guidance addresses people on anticoagulants (SIGN 110; check current status).

candidates.visual_idea: Question card with two questions in large type: 'Did they hit their head?' and 'Do they take a blood thinner?', generic drawn tablet packs with no brand names, and the action: 'Tell 111, the GP or the ambulance crew about the tablet first.'
candidates.pause: Many families know the tablet as 'the blood thinner' and don't know it changes the head injury decision.
candidates.gain: One fact to say first on the phone.
candidates.follow: Short, exact advice that families can act on the same day.

candidates.stimulus_use: The slogan-testing operation was applied to a well-known teaching statistic about long lies; the other words gave nothing extra.
candidates.core_insight: The often-quoted figure that half of people who lie on the floor for over an hour die within six months comes from a small 1981 study and describes an association; newer cohorts still link long lies with serious harm.
candidates.angle: Test the familiar teaching statistic against its source. The case for preventing long lies survives, but on newer evidence and with the right wording: people who can't get up are often already more unwell, so the deaths can't all be put down to the lie.
candidates.position: Teaching about long lies should give the source and size of the 1981 study, describe the link as an association, and cite more recent cohorts.
claims_needing_evidence: Wild, Nayak and Isaacs (BMJ 1981) reported that about half of older people who lay on the floor for more than an hour after a fall died within six months (verify the figure, the sample size and the setting).
The 1981 sample was small and drawn from older people seen by general practitioners after falls at home (verify number and recruitment).
People who can't get up after falling differ from those who can in age, strength and illness, so later deaths can't be attributed to the lie alone (Tinetti 1993 reported characteristics; verify).
A 2008 cohort of people aged over 90 found that lying on the floor for an hour or more was associated with serious injury, hospital admission and moves into long-term care (Fleming 2008, BMJ).

candidates.opening_line_draft: A figure often quoted in falls teaching says that half of people who lie on the floor for over an hour die within six months. It comes from a small study published in 1981.

candidates.pause: Clinicians who have repeated the figure will want to know where it came from.
candidates.gain: A more accurate way to teach about long lies.
candidates.follow: The account traces well-known numbers back to their sources.

candidates.stimulus_use: The son viewpoint and the five-year timescale suggested the slow loss of activity that protective family help can bring; the stated-aim comparison was applied to that help rather than to a formal service.
candidates.core_insight: Giving up activities to avoid falls can reduce strength and balance, so after a fall it helps to ask how an activity could be made safer before deciding to stop it.
candidates.angle: The stated aim of protective help ('I'll do the shopping, you stay in') is safety. Over years, the result can be fewer outings, weaker legs and a higher risk of falling. The trade-off deserves an open conversation in which the older person makes the decision.
candidates.position: Before an older person gives up an activity after a fall, the family and clinicians should ask what makes it risky and whether that part can be changed, and the older person should make the call. (The last part is a judgement about agency, not a finding.)
claims_needing_evidence: Activity restriction because of fear of falling is associated with later decline in physical function (Deshpande 2008, J Am Geriatr Soc).
Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in older people living in the community (Sherrington 2019 Cochrane).
Fear of falling and activity avoidance are common in older people, including people who have not fallen (Scheffer 2008, Age and Ageing systematic review).

candidates.follow: The account deals with real trade-offs without pretending there is a risk-free option.

candidates.stimulus_use: Tracing a handover led to the point where an ambulance crew leaves an older person at home; 'labelling' suggested the non-conveyance record that closes the call.
candidates.working_title: When the ambulance leaves you at home
candidates.core_insight: Many older people who call an ambulance after a fall are checked and left at home, and they should ask for a referral to a falls service so that the reason for the fall is looked into.
candidates.angle: Trace the handover from the ambulance crew to whoever comes next. A call that ends at home is logged as resolved, but the person has the same risk of falling that they had before the crew arrived.
candidates.position: An older person left at home by an ambulance crew after a fall should be referred for a falls assessment, and can ask the crew or the GP for this.

UK ambulance services have pathways for referring older people who fall to community falls services (SAFER 2 trial description; ambulance service pathway documents).
The SAFER 2 trial of a paramedic assessment and referral protocol showed [result to verify] (Snooks 2017, Health Technology Assessment).

candidates.stimulus_use: Tracing a handover with the occupational therapist viewpoint led to equipment moving from ward to home; 'hidden cost' suggested the hands a frame takes up.
candidates.core_insight: A walking aid issued in hospital needs checking in the home where it will be used, because height, doorways and the need to carry things all change how safely it works.
candidates.angle: Follow one piece of equipment from the ward to the kitchen. The hidden cost is that both hands are on the frame, with nothing left for the cup, the pan or the door handle.
candidates.position: Anyone given a walking aid should have it checked at home, including how they will carry things.
claims_needing_evidence: Walking aids can improve balance but also demand attention and arm strength, and can contribute to falls when used incorrectly (Bateni and Maki 2005, Arch Phys Med Rehabil).

Many older people use walking aids that are set at the wrong height or are the wrong type for them (studies of walking aid fit) (unsure of best source).
Wheeled trolley walkers with a tray are one option for carrying things indoors (occupational therapy equipment guidance) (unsure of source).

candidates.pause: A small, familiar difficulty that anyone who has used a frame knows.

candidates.stimulus_use: The smallest-practical-detail operation, with 'light switch' and 'delay', suggested the pendant alarm left on the bedside table at night and the delay that follows.
candidates.working_title: Where is the alarm at 3 a.m.?
candidates.core_insight: A pendant alarm only helps if it is worn when falls happen, including at night and in the bathroom, and if the wearer is willing to press it.
candidates.angle: The smallest practical detail: the pendant on the bedside table, in the drawer, or round the neck of someone who decides not to press it. The gap between owning an alarm and using one can mean hours on the floor.
candidates.position: People with a pendant alarm should wear it day and night, test it regularly, and agree in advance that any time on the floor is a reason to press it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cohort of people aged 90 and over, most of those who had a call alarm did not use it to summon help when they fell alone and couldn't get up ([N to verify]) (Fleming 2008, BMJ).
Reasons for not using alarms include not wearing them, being unable to reach them, and not wanting to trouble anyone (Fleming 2008; qualitative studies) (unsure of qualitative sources).
Some people take pendant alarms off at night or when washing (qualitative or survey studies) (unsure).

candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a drawn bedroom at night with the pendant on the bedside table and the route to the bathroom marked. Three labels: 'Wear it in bed', 'Check whether yours is waterproof and can be worn when washing', 'Press it every time you are on the floor'.
candidates.pause: Families realise the gap may apply to their own parent.
candidates.gain: Three habits that make an alarm work.
candidates.follow: The account deals in small details that prevent harm.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E078 said an alarm should not be the only outcome of a falls clinic; E166 covered bed and chair alarms in hospital. This post is about whether a home pendant alarm is worn and used.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Stocktaking' combined with the first-question operation suggested taking stock of the activities a person has given up.
candidates.working_title: The question about what has stopped
candidates.core_insight: Asking an older person what they have stopped doing because they worry about falling reveals fear and activity restriction that a count of falls misses.
candidates.angle: The first question worth asking after a fall is about the activities dropped since: the regular walk, the bus into town, the bath, the visit to a friend. Taking stock of what has gone shows what to rebuild.
candidates.position: Families and clinicians should ask this question in every conversation about falls.
claims_needing_evidence: The World Falls Guidelines 2022 recommend that falls risk assessment includes concerns about falling (Montero-Odasso 2022).
Concerns about falling are common in older people, including those who have not fallen, and are associated with activity restriction (Scheffer 2008 systematic review).
Activity restriction due to fear of falling is associated with later functional decline (Deshpande 2008).
Validated questionnaires (FES-I and Short FES-I) ask about concern during everyday activities (Yardley 2005; Kempen 2008).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Ask your mother or father this: is there anything you have stopped doing because you are worried about falling?
candidates.visual_idea: Question card with the question in large type and a row of small drawn icons for commonly given-up activities (a walk, a bus trip, a bath, visiting friends), labelled as examples.
candidates.pause: A direct question that readers can use today.
candidates.gain: A way to find hidden restriction and a starting point for help.
candidates.follow: Questions that open useful conversations.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E076 described fear of falling as a disability. This post gives the specific question and what its answer shows; C01-20 covers measurement and treatment for practitioners.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Tailoring' suggested a garment, which led to hip protectors; the change of scale to results per 1000 residents and 'what is left over' (the people who don't wear them) shaped the angle.
candidates.working_title: Hip protectors: a small benefit that depends on wearing them
candidates.core_insight: In care homes, hip protectors probably prevent a small number of hip fractures, mostly among people who wear them consistently; for people living in their own homes, trials have not shown a clear benefit.
candidates.angle: Move from one garment on one person to results per 1000 residents. The benefit is real but small, and what is left over is the group for whom comfort, continence and dressing make wearing them hard.
candidates.position: Hip protectors are a reasonable offer in care homes for people at high risk who find them comfortable, with an honest account of the small absolute benefit; they don't replace falls prevention or bone treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: In nursing care settings, providing hip protectors probably reduces the risk of hip fracture slightly: about [N to verify] fewer hip fractures per 1000 people (Santesso 2014 Cochrane).
For older people living in the community, hip protectors probably have little or no effect on hip fracture (Santesso 2014 Cochrane).
Poor adherence (not wearing the protectors) is a major limitation in the trials (Santesso 2014; Kiel 2007).
Hip protectors may slightly increase the risk of pelvic fracture (Santesso 2014) (unsure).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Hip protectors are padded shields worn over the hips inside underwear, and in care homes they probably prevent a small number of hip fractures.
candidates.visual_idea: Icon array from the Cochrane summary of findings: 1000 care home residents, showing hip fractures with and without protectors, with the denominator and time period labelled; a second small panel states that no clear benefit was shown for people living at home.
candidates.pause: A little-known option presented with a precise, honest number.
candidates.gain: Enough information to discuss with a care home whether to try them.
candidates.follow: Balanced decision support with absolute numbers.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Earlier hip fracture and osteoporosis posts did not discuss hip protectors.

candidates.stimulus_use: The first-question operation combined with 'reversibility' suggested asking when the falls began and what changed just before.
candidates.core_insight: Asking when the falls began and what changed in the weeks before (a new or increased medicine, an illness, a hospital stay, new glasses) is often the quickest route to a reversible cause.
candidates.angle: Timing is the organising question of a falls history. Falls that start at a clear point suggest a trigger that can be reversed, and a trigger such as a new tablet can keep acting while the person waits for a clinic appointment.
candidates.position: Every falls history should record the date the falls started and list changes in the preceding weeks, starting with medicines.
claims_needing_evidence: In older people starting antihypertensive treatment, the risk of hip fracture was higher in the first [N to verify] days after starting (Butt 2012, Arch Intern Med).
Starting some psychotropic medicines, such as benzodiazepines, is associated with a period of raised fracture or falls risk (cohort studies; Wang 2001) (unsure of best source).
The rate of falls is raised in the period after hospital discharge (Mahoney 2000, Arch Intern Med) (unsure).
Expert consensus lists medicines that increase falls risk and should be reviewed in people who fall (STOPPFall, Seppala 2021).
evidence_leads: Butt DA et al. The risk of hip fracture after initiating antihypertensive drugs in the elderly. Arch Intern Med 2012;172:1739-44

candidates.opening_line_draft: The most useful date in a falls history is the date the falls started.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram labelled 'Illustrative example': falls drawn as dots that cluster after one point, with the weeks before that point annotated with possible changes (new tablet, dose increase, infection, hospital stay, new glasses).
candidates.pause: A simple, specific instruction that clinicians can apply in their next history.
candidates.gain: A method for finding reversible causes sooner.
candidates.follow: Clinical teaching points that are easy to use.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E064 lists possible causes to ask about; E071 and E145 cover sedatives. This post teaches the onset date as the organising question and does not repeat the drug-specific arguments.

candidates.stimulus_use: Applying the standard offer to the poorest or most isolated person, with 'bus pass' and 'signposting', led to the question of who can't reach falls prevention classes.
candidates.core_insight: Community strength and balance classes reach fewer of the people who are poorest, most isolated or housebound, and home-based programmes exist that reduce falls.
candidates.angle: Apply the usual offer (a leaflet listing classes) to the person with no car, a bus route that doesn't go there, a fee they can't spare, and no one to go with. For that person the leaflet is not an offer.
candidates.position: Falls services should offer home-based programmes and help with transport to people who can't reach classes. (Judgement, marked as such.)
claims_needing_evidence: Uptake of and adherence to community falls prevention exercise are lower in some groups (characteristics to verify, e.g. socioeconomic status, living alone, health) (Nyman and Victor 2012, Age and Ageing).
Home-based strength and balance programmes such as Otago reduce falls in older people (Campbell 1997, BMJ).
In a trial of people who had fallen and attended a falls clinic, a home-based exercise programme reduced subsequent falls by [N to verify] over 12 months (Liu-Ambrose 2019, JAMA).
Programme factors such as transport, cost and location are associated with adherence to group falls exercise (systematic review; McPhate 2013) (unsure).

candidates.opening_line_draft: A leaflet listing strength and balance classes is an offer only to people who can get to them.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a drawn local map with a class venue and three homes at different distances, one near a bus stop, one with no bus route, one where the person is housebound; beside it, three options (transport, home-based programme, class). No numbers.
candidates.pause: A plain fairness point that services and families recognise.
candidates.gain: Knowing that home-based programmes exist and can be asked for.
candidates.follow: The account pays attention to who services miss.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E083 said to ask what programmes exist locally and to call their absence a commissioning failure. This post is about who can't reach what exists, and names the evidence for home-based options.

candidates.core_insight: Calling a fall 'mechanical' records how it happened, but even a trip has causes in the person (foot clearance, speed of the recovery step, vision, attention, strength) that an assessment should look for.
candidates.angle: A common documentation shortcut that needs qualifying. A trip in a fit 40-year-old and a trip in a frail 85-year-old are different events: why didn't the foot clear the edge, and why didn't the recovery step prevent the fall?
candidates.position: Clinicians should replace 'mechanical fall' in the notes with a short description of what happened and what was checked.
claims_needing_evidence: 'Mechanical fall' has no agreed clinical definition (falls terminology literature; commentary articles) (unsure of source).
Older adults have slower and less effective stepping responses after a trip, which makes a trip more likely to end in a fall (Pavol 2001; Maki and McIlroy 2006).
Reduced toe clearance during walking is associated with trips in older people (gait biomechanics studies) (unsure of best source).
A multifactorial falls assessment includes gait, balance, vision, medicines and cognition (NICE NG249; World Falls Guidelines 2022).
evidence_leads: Pavol MJ et al. Mechanisms leading to a fall from an induced trip in healthy older adults. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2001;56:M428-37

NICE NG249 (2025); Montero-Odasso M et al. Age Ageing 2022
candidates.opening_line_draft: 'Mechanical fall' in the notes tells the next doctor how the person hit the ground, and nothing about why.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a drawn trip over a doorway threshold, with labels at each point where the person's body is involved: toe clearance, the recovery step, seeing the edge, attention, leg strength. Heading: 'Even a trip has causes to look for'.
candidates.pause: Practitioners have written or read the phrase this week.
candidates.gain: A better way to document a fall and a list of what to check.
candidates.follow: Teaching that sharpens everyday clinical language.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E064 told families that a fall is a medical event until someone asks why. This post is for clinicians and examines the specific phrase and the trip itself.

candidates.core_insight: When falls in care homes were filmed, the commonest cause was incorrect shifting of body weight during ordinary movements such as walking, turning and sitting down, and trips were less common.
candidates.angle: A finding that should change how care home staff think about falls: most filmed falls did not involve the floor or an obstacle, and the risky moments were transfers, turns and sitting down.
candidates.position: Care home falls prevention should put as much effort into supporting transfers, turning and sitting down as into removing trip hazards.
claims_needing_evidence: Robinovitch and colleagues (Lancet 2013) analysed [N to verify] falls captured on video among [N to verify] residents of two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada.

The most frequent cause was incorrect weight shifting ([N to verify]%), followed by trip or stumble ([N to verify]%), with hit or bump, loss of support and collapse each accounting for about [N to verify]%.
Falls occurred most often during walking forward, standing and sitting down (percentages to verify).
Limitations: two facilities in one country, cameras in common areas rather than bedrooms or bathrooms (verify from the paper).
evidence_leads: Robinovitch SN et al. Video capture of the circumstances of falls in elderly people residing in long-term care: an observational study. Lancet 2013;381:47-54
Yang Y et al. Follow-up analyses of the same video dataset, e.g. head impact during falls in long-term care (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: When researchers filmed [N to verify] falls in two Canadian care homes, the commonest cause was incorrect shifting of body weight during ordinary movements; trips were less common.
candidates.visual_idea: Horizontal bar chart built only from the paper's published percentages of fall causes, labelled with the number of falls and residents, the setting and the year, and a note that cameras were in common areas.
candidates.pause: A surprising, specific finding with a strong visual.
candidates.gain: A different picture of where to focus effort in care homes.
candidates.follow: The account brings useful research into everyday practice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E082 covered medical review of care home residents who fall. This post reports how falls happen in care homes and does not repeat that argument.

candidates.working_title: How afraid, and how at risk?
candidates.core_insight: How afraid someone is of falling and how likely they are to fall often don't match, and each mismatch calls for a different kind of help.
candidates.angle: A 2010 cohort combined perceived and physical risk into four groups. The anxious person with low physical risk and the unworried person with high physical risk are both missed by an assessment that measures only one of the two.
candidates.position: Falls assessment should measure both concern about falling and physical risk, and match help to the combination.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cohort of [N to verify] community-dwelling older people in Sydney, about [N to verify] had a mismatch between perceived and physiological falls risk (Delbaere 2010, BMJ).
The group with low physiological risk but high perceived risk was associated with depressive symptoms, neuroticism and poorer executive function (verify from the paper).
Perceived risk was associated with later falls independently of physiological risk (verify).
The group with high physiological risk and low perceived risk had [characteristics to verify].
evidence_leads: Delbaere K, Close JCT, Brodaty H, Sachdev P, Lord SR. Determinants of disparities between perceived and physiological risk of falling among elderly people: cohort study. BMJ 2010;341:c4165
Lord SR, Menz HB, Tiedemann A. A physiological profile approach to falls risk assessment and prevention. Phys Ther 2003;83:237-52
candidates.opening_line_draft: Fear of falling and the physical risk of falling often don't match. In one cohort, [N to verify] of older people were anxious despite a low physical risk, or unworried despite a high one.
candidates.visual_idea: 2 by 2 grid: physical risk (low, high) against concern about falling (low, high). Each cell shows the paper's group name and, if verified, its share, with one line on the kind of help that fits.
candidates.pause: A grid readers can place themselves or a parent in.
candidates.gain: An explanation of why reassurance helps one person and exercise helps another.
candidates.follow: Research explained in a form people can use.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E076 treated fear of falling as a disability. This post is about the mismatch between fear and physical risk, which no earlier post covered.

candidates.working_title: Fear of falling has its own treatment
candidates.core_insight: Concern about falling can be measured with a short validated questionnaire and reduced by exercise and by cognitive behavioural programmes that include graded practice of avoided activities.
candidates.angle: Fear of falling is often treated as a side effect that should settle once falls are addressed. For practitioners it deserves its own measurement and its own intervention, with trial evidence for both.
candidates.position: When concern about falling is high, practitioners should measure it and offer an intervention aimed at it, alongside falls prevention.
claims_needing_evidence: Exercise probably reduces fear of falling to a small to moderate degree immediately after the intervention (Kendrick 2014 Cochrane).
Cognitive behavioural interventions reduce fear of falling in older people, in a meta-analysis of trials (Liu 2018, Age and Ageing).
A multicomponent cognitive behavioural group programme reduced concerns about falls and activity avoidance in a Dutch randomised trial (Zijlstra 2009, J Am Geriatr Soc).
The Short FES-I has 7 items and is validated for measuring concern about falling (Kempen 2008, Age and Ageing).
The World Falls Guidelines 2022 recommend assessing concerns about falling (Montero-Odasso 2022).
evidence_leads: Kendrick D et al. Exercise for reducing fear of falling in older people living in the community. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD009848

Kempen GI et al. The Short FES-I. Age Ageing 2008;37:45-50

Parry SW et al. Cognitive-behavioural therapy-based intervention to reduce fear of falling in older people: therapy development and randomised controlled trial (STRIDE). Health Technol Assess 2016;20(56) (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Fear of falling can be measured with a seven-item questionnaire and treated with graded practice of the activities a person now avoids.
candidates.visual_idea: Flow diagram: 'Ask about concern' to 'Measure (Short FES-I)' to 'Offer strength and balance exercise plus graded practice of avoided activities' to 'Measure again'; source credits in the footer.
candidates.pause: Practitioners who think of fear of falling as a feeling see that it has a measure and a treatment.
candidates.gain: A concrete pathway for a common problem.
candidates.follow: The account shows which care works and how to deliver it.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E076 asked whether a programme exists. This post is for practitioners on measurement and on the specific treatments with trial evidence; C01-13 gives the public-facing question.

candidates.core_insight: If you fall and can't get up, keeping warm, calling or signalling for help, and changing position every so often reduce the harm of a long wait on the floor.
candidates.angle: Most falls advice is about prevention. This is about the hour on the floor, and the small preparations (a phone carried in a pocket, a blanket or throw within reach at floor level) that make it bearable and shorter.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: NHS or Age UK guidance advises people who can't get up after a fall to call for help, cover themselves to keep warm, and move position regularly while waiting (verify exact wording and source).
Long periods on the floor are associated with pressure damage, dehydration, hypothermia and muscle breakdown (clinical reviews).
Carrying a mobile phone or wearing an alarm allows a person to call for help from the floor (public guidance).
evidence_leads: NHS website: Falls, including what to do if you fall (unsure of page title)
NHS inform (Scotland): Falls page (unsure)
Age UK: Staying steady or Get up and go guide (unsure of title)
Fleming J, Brayne C. BMJ 2008;337:a2227 (for how often people are unable to get up)
candidates.opening_line_draft: If you fall and can't get up, keep warm, call for help and change position every so often while you wait.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card with four drawn icons taken from one verified guide: call or signal for help, cover yourself to keep warm, shift position every so often, move away from anything wet or cold; a footer note to keep a phone on you.
candidates.pause: A practical instruction that most people have never read.
candidates.gain: A plan for the worst hour.
candidates.follow: Calm, practical advice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. No earlier post addressed what to do while on the floor.

candidates.working_title: After a long lie, write down the hours
candidates.core_insight: Time on the floor changes the checks needed after a fall: skin, temperature, fluids, kidney function and creatine kinase for muscle breakdown.
candidates.angle: Record the time the person was found and the time they were last seen well, then check the complications that come from lying still as well as the injuries that come from landing.
candidates.position: Every assessment after a fall should record how long the person was on the floor and, after a long lie, check pressure areas, temperature, hydration, kidney function and creatine kinase.
claims_needing_evidence: A long lie is commonly defined as remaining on the floor for an hour or more after a fall (Fleming 2008; research definitions).
Complications of a long lie include pressure injury, dehydration, hypothermia, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury and pneumonia (clinical reviews).
Rhabdomyolysis is detected by a raised creatine kinase and can cause acute kidney injury (Bosch 2009, N Engl J Med).
Pressure damage can develop within hours on a hard surface (pressure ulcer guidance; NICE CG179) (verify the time frame).
evidence_leads: Fleming J, Brayne C. BMJ 2008;337:a2227
Bosch X, Poch E, Grau JM. Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. N Engl J Med 2009;361:62-72
NICE CG179. Pressure ulcers: prevention and management (2014)
A systematic or scoping review of long lies in older people (unsure; search needed)
candidates.opening_line_draft: After a long lie, the first number to write down is how many hours the person was on the floor.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a drawn person lying on their side with labelled check points (pressure areas on the lower hip, shoulder and heel; temperature; fluids; blood tests for kidney function and creatine kinase), and two boxes: 'Time found' and 'Last seen well'.
candidates.pause: Clinicians see a concrete detail that is easy to miss.
candidates.gain: A checklist for a common presentation.
candidates.follow: Teaching that improves the next assessment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E058 covered hidden fractures after unwitnessed falls. This post is about complications of time on the floor, which no earlier post covered.

candidates.core_insight: Varifocal and bifocal glasses blur the ground near your feet, and a trial found that single-vision distance glasses for walking outside reduced falls in people who went out often, while outdoor falls rose in people who rarely went out.
candidates.angle: A sensible-sounding change with an honest subgroup result: the benefit depended on how much the person was out and about, and the overall result did not show a clear difference.
candidates.position: For older people who wear varifocals and walk outside a lot, a separate pair of distance glasses for walking is worth discussing with an optometrist; it is not a change to make for everyone.
claims_needing_evidence: Multifocal glasses impair edge-contrast sensitivity and depth perception in the lower visual field, and multifocal wearers had more falls in one cohort (Lord 2002, J Am Geriatr Soc).
In the VISIBLE trial of [N to verify] regular multifocal wearers, providing single-lens distance glasses did not clearly reduce falls overall (Haran 2010, BMJ).

In a planned subgroup who took part in regular outdoor activities, the intervention reduced falls, particularly outdoor falls; in those with little outdoor activity, outdoor falls increased (verify direction, size and whether the subgroup was prespecified).

candidates.pause: A physical experience many readers recognise.
candidates.gain: A specific conversation to have with the optometrist, and its limits.
candidates.follow: Balanced reading of trials that handles subgroups accurately.
candidates.earlier_overlap: No earlier post covered glasses and falls. Possible overlap with C14 (vision) in this collection; allocate to one category.

candidates.core_insight: An older person who stops walking to answer a question may need their full attention to walk; a small 1997 study linked this sign with falls, and later work found it specific but insensitive.
candidates.angle: A famous bedside sign from a small study: useful when present, weak as reassurance when absent. The post teaches how much weight a sign like this can carry.
candidates.position: Treat stopping walking when talking as a prompt for a fuller falls assessment; its absence gives little reassurance.
claims_needing_evidence: In a 1997 study of [N to verify] residents of residential care in Umea, Sweden, [N to verify] of the [N to verify] who stopped walking when talking fell within six months, compared with [N to verify] of those who kept walking (Lundin-Olsson 1997, Lancet).
A later systematic review found that stopping walking while talking had high specificity and low sensitivity for predicting falls (Beauchet 2009, Eur J Neurol) (verify).
Gait slows more under a second task (dual-task walking) in people at higher falls risk (dual-task literature; Muir-Hunter 2016) (unsure).

candidates.visual_idea: Comic strip, 3 panels, labelled 'Illustrative': a physiotherapist walks beside an older man in a corridor and asks a question; he stops to answer; a caption panel gives the study size and what the sign can and can't tell you.
candidates.pause: A moment clinicians see every day.
candidates.gain: A quick sign and how much weight to give it.
candidates.follow: The account teaches how to judge the evidence behind bedside signs.

candidates.working_title: Is it the right kind of class?
candidates.core_insight: Exercise that reduces falls challenges standing balance, gets harder over time and continues for months; a class done sitting down has other benefits but is not the kind shown to prevent falls.
candidates.angle: A public explanation turned into questions to ask before joining a class, so that people choose one that matches the evidence.
candidates.position: Older people choosing an exercise class to prevent falls should ask whether it includes standing balance work, gets progressively harder, and runs several times a week for months.
claims_needing_evidence: Programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises reduce falls; the evidence for walking alone, dance or resistance training alone is uncertain (Sherrington 2019 Cochrane).
In a meta-analysis, programmes with a high challenge to balance and more than 3 hours a week had larger effects (Sherrington 2017, Br J Sports Med) (verify).

The World Falls Guidelines recommend progressive balance and functional exercise with resistance training, at least 3 times a week, continued for at least 12 weeks and ideally longer (Montero-Odasso 2022) (verify wording).
The UK Chief Medical Officers advise older adults to do activities that improve strength and balance on at least two days a week (UK CMO guidelines 2019).
Seated exercise has not been shown to reduce falls (Sherrington reviews) (verify wording; seated work may be a starting point for frailer people).

candidates.core_insight: Urgency incontinence is linked with falls and fractures in older people, so a falls assessment should ask about the bladder, and urgency can often be treated.
candidates.angle: An embarrassing symptom that people rarely mention unprompted; asking about it can uncover a treatable contributor to falls, and first-line treatment does not need a sedating medicine.
candidates.position: Every falls assessment should ask about urinary urgency, and people with urgency should be offered assessment and treatment, starting with measures such as bladder training.
claims_needing_evidence: In the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures, women with weekly or more frequent urge incontinence had a higher risk of falls and non-spine fractures (Brown 2000, J Am Geriatr Soc) (numbers to verify).
A systematic review found that urinary incontinence, particularly urge incontinence, is associated with falls (Chiarelli 2009) (verify).
Bladder training is a first-line treatment for urgency incontinence in women (NICE NG123); guidance for men is separate (NICE CG97).
Nocturia is associated with falls in older people (cohort studies; Stewart 1992) (unsure).

candidates.pause: A link most readers haven't made.
candidates.gain: A symptom to mention and a treatment to ask about.

candidates.core_insight: Some patterns of walking and falling point to a specific diagnosis: early backward falls in progressive supranuclear palsy, broad shuffling steps with urinary urgency and slowed thinking in normal pressure hydrocephalus, or unsteadiness with eyes closed in sensory neuropathy.
candidates.angle: Falls as a symptom of something else. Watching a person walk, turn and stand with eyes closed can reveal a named, sometimes treatable condition behind a label of 'gait problems of old age'.
candidates.position: Clinicians should watch every person who falls walk, turn and stand with eyes closed, and consider named conditions before putting gait problems down to age.
claims_needing_evidence: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of onset are a core clinical feature in the Movement Disorder Society criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (Hoglinger 2017, Mov Disord).
The MDS criteria for Parkinson's disease count recurrent falls due to impaired balance within 3 years of onset as a feature that argues against the diagnosis (Postuma 2015, Mov Disord).

Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, often with urinary urgency and cognitive change, and some people improve after shunt surgery (Relkin 2005; Nakajima 2021 guidelines).
A positive Romberg test indicates loss of position sense, as in peripheral neuropathy or vitamin B12 deficiency (neurology texts; Snijders 2007 review).

candidates.gain: A structured way to watch gait.
candidates.follow: High-yield clinical teaching.

candidates.core_insight: A slow collection of blood between the brain and the skull (chronic subdural haematoma) can follow even a minor knock to the head and show itself weeks later as unsteadiness, headache, drowsiness or slower thinking, and it is treatable.
candidates.angle: A fall can be the cause and, weeks later, the symptom. New unsteadiness in the weeks after a fall should prompt a question about the head, especially in someone on a blood thinner.
candidates.position: If an older person becomes newly unsteady, drowsy, weak on one side or slower in thinking in the weeks after a fall or knock to the head, the family should tell the GP about the fall and ask whether a scan is needed.
claims_needing_evidence: Chronic subdural haematoma is more common in older people and often follows a minor head injury, which may not be remembered (Kolias 2014, Nat Rev Neurol).
Symptoms typically develop over weeks and include headache, gait disturbance and falls, cognitive change, drowsiness and limb weakness (Kolias 2014).
Anticoagulant and antiplatelet medicines are risk factors (Kolias 2014).
Surgical drainage is the main treatment for symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma, and a large trial found dexamethasone led to worse outcomes than placebo (Hutchinson 2020, N Engl J Med).

candidates.core_insight: Bed rails can stop someone rolling out of bed but can't stop someone who wants to get up and may climb over them, so the decision should be made for each person.
candidates.angle: A trade-off between safety and restriction. A systematic review did not find that bed rails increase falls overall, while entrapment and climbing risks are real for some people. Blanket rules in either direction fail someone.
candidates.position: Bed rail decisions should be made person by person, based on whether the person might roll out and whether they will try to climb over, with alternatives such as a low bed considered; neither blanket use nor blanket bans.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of clinical studies found no clear evidence that bed rails increase falls or injury overall, and serious injury from bed rails was rare (Healey 2008, Age and Ageing) (verify conclusions).
MHRA guidance describes the risks of entrapment and of falls from a greater height when people climb over bed rails, and advises individual risk assessment (MHRA bed rails guidance).
Low beds and crash mats are used as alternatives in hospitals and care homes (MHRA guidance) (unsure).
Using bed rails to stop a person leaving bed can count as restraint under UK care regulation (CQC or Care Inspectorate guidance) (unsure).

candidates.core_insight: Trials of withdrawing medicines that increase falls risk have given mixed results, partly because withdrawal often doesn't happen or doesn't last, so a medication review needs follow-up to check that the change held.
candidates.angle: An intervention whose benefit is commonly overstated. Medication review is often presented as the easiest win in falls prevention; the trial evidence is more mixed, and carrying the change through is the weak point.
candidates.position: Medication review in people who fall is still worthwhile where a specific drug is causing harm, and clinicians should check some weeks later that stopped medicines have stayed stopped.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised trial, gradual withdrawal of psychotropic medicines reduced falls in older people, and many participants restarted the medicines after the trial ended (Campbell 1999, J Am Geriatr Soc) (numbers to verify).

The IMPROveFALL trial of withdrawing fall-risk-increasing drugs in older people attending an ED after a fall did not show a clear reduction in falls (Boye 2017, Age and Ageing) (verify, including how many drugs were actually withdrawn).
A systematic review of deprescribing fall-risk-increasing drugs found [result to verify] (Lee 2021, BMJ Open) (unsure).
Expert consensus lists fall-risk-increasing drugs and how to deprescribe them (STOPPFall, Seppala 2021, Age and Ageing).

candidates.core_insight: People often forget falls within months, so a short note of each fall (date, time, what they were doing, how they felt just before, whether they could get up) gives the clinician a pattern that memory loses.
candidates.angle: A small practical detail with an evidence base: falls research uses diaries and calendars because recall is unreliable, and families can do the same at home.
candidates.position: Older people who have fallen, or their families, should keep a written note of every fall and take it to appointments.
claims_needing_evidence: When asked after 12 months, [N to verify] of older people with a confirmed fall did not recall it (Cummings 1988, J Am Geriatr Soc).
Falls research recommends prospective recording with daily diaries or calendars returned monthly, because recall is unreliable (Lamb 2005, ProFaNE consensus).
The circumstances of a fall (time, activity, symptoms beforehand) help identify its cause (NICE NG249 or World Falls Guidelines on the falls history) (verify wording).
